sections.h2: Where to record a deed in Yuma County
sections.html:
Bring or send the deed to the Recorder's Office, 298 S. Main Street in Yuma (ZIP 85364). The county calls this a new address, and a few older county pages still carry a different street number, so trust the one printed here. The counter opens at 8:00 a.m. and closes at 5:00 p.m., Monday through Friday, and you can reach staff at (928) 373-6020. If you are carrying a signed deed in on closing day, a quick call first saves a wasted trip.

The Recorder keeps the county's public record and also runs voter registration and early voting. Deeds do not go to the Assessor or the Treasurer, who share a separate building at 197 S. Main Street. Think of the three offices this way: the Recorder files the paper, the Assessor tracks parcel values and ownership, and the Treasurer sends the tax bill and takes payment.

You can file in person, by mail or electronically. Title and escrow companies nearly always record electronically. Private owners handling their own paperwork usually walk the paper deed to the counter.

MethodHow it works
In personWalk up to the counter at 298 South Main Street in Yuma, open 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. Monday to Friday
By mailMark the envelope Attention: Recording Division, use the street address above, and include a check or money order payable to Yuma County Recorder
ElectronicA private vendor sends the file for you. The county names five: Data Services, Inc., eRecording Partners Network, Indecomm Global Services, CSC eRecording and Simplifile

The county runs no portal of its own for electronic filing, so contact one of those providers directly. If you are mailing, phone the office first for the current recording fee and a list of what belongs in the envelope. When a title company closes your sale, the recording charge shows up as a line on your settlement statement.

Any deed that moves title needs an Affidavit of Real Property Value. A.R.S. 11-1133 is the rule. Either party, or an agent acting for one of them, certifies the facts on a Department of Revenue form. Without a complete affidavit, the recorder must turn the deed away, unless the deed is marked exempt.

The Assessor later reads these forms to update the parcel record, which is why they ask so much:

  • who the buyer and seller are, how to reach each, and where the tax bill should be mailed
  • how the parcel is described legally, plus its street address and assessor's parcel number
  • the sale date, what was paid in total, how much of it was cash up front and how the loan is structured
  • whether buyer and seller are related, and whether the buyer will live there or rent it out

A few transfers skip the affidavit. Under A.R.S. 11-1134, the list covers gifts, court-ordered conveyances, quitclaims with no money involved, confirmation or correction deeds, deeds creating survivorship joint tenancy, and trustee's deeds following a deed of trust. Whichever one you claim must be written on the deed. The Recorder's staff can walk you through the affidavit and the exemption codes if the form looks confusing.

The Recorder posts answers to 23 common questions. Several apply directly to a seller:

  • checking a property for liens and ordering a copy of a deed
  • putting a name on or taking a name off a property, and moving property into or out of a trust
  • changing who owns a parcel
  • what a declaration of homestead does
  • how to look up a house in foreclosure
  • recording requirements and the usual reasons a document comes back rejected
  • notary service at the office

Over at the Assessor, the FAQ confirms that deed copies come from the Recorder and that sale prices and owners can be searched online. A manufactured home or recreational vehicle that is not attached to land gets retitled at the Motor Vehicle Division, 2165 E. Gila Ridge Road, Yuma 85365, and the county is not involved.

sections.h2: Property tax and liens at closing
sections.html:
Unpaid tax follows the property, not the person. Under A.R.S. 42-17153, a lien for each year's tax takes hold every January 1. It outranks most other claims on the parcel, apart from state liens and liens for other years' taxes. Expect your title company to ask the Treasurer for a payoff number before the deed goes on record.

Each bill comes in two installments. The second installment of 2026 tax is due March 1, 2027 and turns delinquent after May 3, 2027. Any 2025 tax still unpaid gets a 5 percent penalty on January 1, 2027, and a lien sale for those years is scheduled for February 18, 2027. Paying by 5:00 p.m. on February 17 keeps a parcel out of it.

The Treasurer, at (928) 539-7781, can quote what you owe. Not sure how the county has coded your home? The Assessor's Notice of Value explains the codes for owner-occupied residences versus rentals.

Yuma County takes up the southwestern corner of Arizona. The 2020 census counted 203,881 residents, and the county seat is the city of Yuma. Other incorporated places are the cities of San Luis and Somerton and the Town of Wellton, with Dateland as an unincorporated community.

The county's website offers recorder forms and a search of recorded documents under the Recorder's menu. For owner names, parcel numbers and sale data, use the Assessor's online records at yumacountyaz-assessor.tylerhost.net/assessor/web. Pull up your parcel there before you complete the affidavit so the numbers match.

A little preparation keeps a Yuma County closing moving.

  1. Look up your parcel on the Assessor's site and compare the parcel number and legal description with the deed.
  2. Settle who records. A title company will e-record. If you file it yourself, plan on the counter or the mail.
  3. Complete the affidavit in full, or identify the exemption that fits and write it on the deed.
  4. Request a tax payoff from the Treasurer before the closing date.
  5. Save a copy of the recorded deed when it is returned.

A cash sale has no lender paperwork, but the deed, the affidavit and the tax payoff still have to be in order. Recording works the same way whoever the buyer is, and it is the step that makes the new owner official in the public record.

Most Yuma sales follow the same rhythm. The buyer and seller sign a purchase contract, the title company opens an order, and a payoff request goes out to the Treasurer so no tax surprise appears late. Near the end, you sign the deed in front of a notary, and the affidavit is completed alongside it. The title company then sends everything to be recorded, often within a day, and releases your proceeds once the deed is on the public record.

If you sell on your own, you carry more of these steps yourself: the signing, the affidavit, the trip or envelope to the Recorder and the tax payoff. None of them is hard, but each has a form or a fee attached, which is why a short phone call to the office beforehand pays off.

Recorders turn away documents for ordinary reasons: a missing affidavit, an exemption that is not written on the deed, a check made out to the wrong payee, or a mailing package without a return address. The Recorder's FAQ has an entry on the most common rejection reasons, so read it before you file, or phone the counter and ask what trips people up.

A rejected deed delays the moment the buyer's name appears in the record, and that can hold up the sale funds. If you have a closing date, start the call to the office a few days early. Then ask your title company, escrow officer or attorney to check the legal description one more time against the parcel record.

faqs.q: Where is the Yuma County Recorder's office?
faqs.a: Go to 298 S. Main Street in Yuma. Staff are there from 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. on workdays and answer at (928) 373-6020. Envelopes should be marked for the Recording Division.

faqs.q: Can I record a deed electronically in Yuma County?
faqs.a: Yes, but only through a private vendor the county names, such as Simplifile or CSC eRecording. Pick one and contact it directly, since the county does not take e-filings itself.

faqs.q: How much does Yuma County charge to record a deed?
faqs.a: The amount changes, so phone (928) 373-6020 before you mail anything. Send a check or money order made out to Yuma County Recorder. If a title company is closing for you, the charge is itemized in your settlement paperwork.

faqs.q: Does a Yuma County deed need an affidavit of property value?
faqs.a: In most cases. State law requires the affidavit on any deed that transfers title, and an incomplete one gets refused. Gifts and a handful of other transfers are exempt, but the deed has to say which exemption applies.

faqs.q: How do I get a copy of my Yuma County deed?
faqs.a: Request it from the Recorder. A quick call will tell you how to submit the request and whether a copy fee applies.
